newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh carpet maker wants to expand globally.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh carpet maker wants to expand globally.

text.p: Bangladesh, one of the world's poorest countries, was once renowned for its golden jute but for many years was virtually pushed out of the world market because of growing competition from cheaper synthetics.
Now, the world is again looking to the south Asian country for its finely textured, colourful, durable and environment-friendly jute carpets.

"Prospects of jute carpets are very very good. If we can properly plan and explore the world market, we can use our entire jute production in the carpet industry alone," said Shahnewaz Chowdhury, managing director of the Saleh Group of Industries that owns two carpet factories in the port city of Chittagong.
"We can then offer better price to jute growers, earn more foreign exchange and largely contribute towards development of the country," he told Reuters this past week.
His father Saleh Ahmed Chowdhury, who died in 1986, founded the group.
"Bangladesh did not know the full use of the jute. We are lucky to have such a fine fibre and luckier because of late we have found its use if making carpets," the son said.
Chowdhury, 37, a fomer member of parliament, was flushed with confidence as he sat in a sprawling, poshly-decorated living roon, with a full-size leopard skin hanging on the wall.
He said his overseas business had become so lucrative that he had decided to quit active politics and to devote his full time to entrepreneurship only.
"We are born businessmen," he said. "My father, who started as an export-import trader, visioned that the world is changing. The people are returning to nature.
"So he set up the country's first carpet mill in 1978."
"We can perhaps now hit a gold mine... provided quality of the carpets is guaranteed. I personally take special care about quality. I am the last one to compromise it," he said.
His two carpet units, which employ about 2,000 workers, exported $7.5 million worth of carpets in fiscal 1995-96 (July-June), mostly to Britain.
"I am expecting a higher turnover at about $10 million in 1996-97," he said.
Other countries to which the Saleh group exports includes Australia, the United States, Taiwan, Canada, Japan and Kuwait.
Chowdhury currently has three overseas business offices -- in the United States, Scotland and Singapore -- and plans to expand further.

"We are meeting only a fraction of the world demand for natural-fibre carpets. The demand is growing fast. Wooden floor (in houses and offices) is a modern fashion and jute rugs are the best option for wall-to-wall decoration," he said.

Chowdhury pointed out several pluses for Bangladesh's carpet industry. "We offer products at a cheap rate ($9.5 per sq-metre), dyed with health hazard-free chemicals, and we don't use child labour," he said.
He denied having any major labour problems but said competition from carpet makers in Belgium, India and China was getting tougher.
"Despite a growing consciousness in favour of environment-friendly carpets, rugs, sacks and packing sheets, synthetics makers like Exxon, Dubont, Mobil etc are keeping up market pressure.
"But I am sure we can penetrate (the markets) effectively with better marketing strategy and by maintaining quality."
Afroza Akhtari, chief designer of the two carpet plants, said she designs according to buyer's choice and had never confronted any complaint.
"It's a two-way traffic. We offer them a variety of designs we do ourselves for a choice and they also come up with their own ideas. We go for buyers' satisfaction."
Akhtari said 90 percent of the raw materials used in carpet making was jute and 10 percent cotton.
All dyes are imported from Switzerland, Germany and other European countries at a higher price than would be available in regional countries to ensure they are not injurious to health.
Sakhawat Hossain, accounts manager of the group, said the two carpet units had a total production capacity of 900,000 sq-metres of carpets annually.
"It's just less than a quarter of the demand we receive from buyers," he told Reuters.
Chowdhury claimed that Saleh Group was the biggest private sector exporter of carpets from Bangladesh.
"We have not taken any foreign aid for setting up or expanding our business. We are hundred percent Bangladeshi and want to stay so, at least in the immediate future."
